screens.title: Smart Pointers and Resource Management (RAII)
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will learn why raw pointers create fragile programs and how smart pointers, using the RAII principle, make resource management automatic and reliable. You'll see the two main ownership models: exclusive ownership with unique pointers, and shared ownership with reference-counted shared pointers. We will also examine the subtle circular dependency problem that can occur with shared ownership and how weak pointers provide a carefully scoped, non-owning reference to solve it. Along the way we'll walk through real C++ examples that show construction, destruction, transfer of ownership, and reference counting in action. You will understand when to prefer make_unique or make_shared, how move semantics preserve exclusive ownership, and when to opt for weak_ptr to break cycles. By the end, you'll know practical rules of thumb for choosing the right smart pointer for file handles, graph nodes, containers, and APIs. This knowledge reduces memory leaks, eliminates dangling pointers, and makes your code safer under exceptions. Ready to see how RAII turns lifetime management from a manual chore into a design principle you can rely on? Let's explore the key topics and examples that will make this concrete.

Smart Pointers and RAII

Understand ownership models in C++ and how smart pointers use RAII to manage dynamic memory safely, even across exceptions.

Why this matters

Automatic cleanup prevents leaks and crashes, and makes ownership explicit in interfaces.

Concept Map
RAII
Acquire in constructor, release in destructor.
unique_ptr
Exclusive ownership, move-only.
shared_ptr
Reference counted shared ownership.
Explore Key Topics
Ownership patterns
Decide between exclusive and shared ownership based on who must control lifetimes.
Breaking cycles
Use weak_ptr for non-owning back-references to avoid memory leaks.
Practical patterns
Prefer make_unique and make_shared for safety and efficiency.
Quick Visual
Object lifetime
Destructor releases the resource when the owner goes out of scope.
What you'll practice
Creating unique_ptr and shared_ptr, transferring ownership, and using weak_ptr to avoid leaks in graphs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide our practice so you can measure real competency. First, you'll identify the common hazards of raw pointers: memory leaks when delete is forgotten, and dangling pointers when memory is accessed after deletion. Recognizing these bugs is the first step to avoiding them. Second, you'll explain the RAII principle: acquire a resource in a constructor and release it in the destructor. This single idea underpins reliable cleanup even when exceptions are thrown. Third, you'll implement and use std::unique_ptr for exclusive ownership: create objects with make_unique, move ownership, and avoid copies. That gives you a safe replacement for raw pointers when a single object owns a resource. Fourth, you'll implement and use std::shared_ptr and std::weak_ptr: observe how shared_ptr increments and decrements a reference counter, know when shared ownership is appropriate, and use weak_ptr to break circular references. Each skill is paired with code examples and a small mnemonic to help you choose the right pointer type in practical contexts. By training these four skills you reduce leaks and make C++ lifetimes explicit and maintainable.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Practice Patterns

Practice & Patterns

Small experiments confirm ownership behavior and destructor timing. Use console messages to observe lifetimes.

Pattern
Observe destructors

Add print statements in constructors and destructors to confirm when objects are created and destroyed under different ownership scenarios.

Mnemonic
Owner counts

Think: unique means one owner; shared means a counter, weak means a peek that doesn't increase the count.

Verification
Small tests to run
  • Move a unique_ptr and confirm the source becomes null and destructor runs once.
  • Copy a shared_ptr, push into a vector, and print use_count at each step.
  • Create mutual references and then switch one to weak_ptr to observe destruction.

screens.title: The cost of raw pointers
screens.narratorSegment: Before we adopt smart pointers, we must understand what can go wrong with raw pointers. Raw pointers require manual calls to delete for every new. Forgetting a delete produces a memory leak: the program holds memory it no longer needs and never returns it to the system. Over time, leaks accumulate and can exhaust memory. Another hazard is dangling pointers: if memory is deleted but a pointer still refers to that address, dereferencing it causes undefined behavior and can crash the program. These bugs are often intermittent and hard to trace. A common debugging pattern is to add logging in constructors and destructors to observe when objects are freed, but prevention is better than diagnosis. Consider this minimal example that intentionally leaks memory. It allocates, but never releases the object. Run this small program in a controlled environment to watch how destructor messages never appear and how memory remains allocated. The key takeaway is that manual pairing of new and delete is error-prone, especially across exceptions, early returns, or complex control flow. That fragility is the reason RAII and smart pointers are such powerful patterns: they move cleanup out of your head and into object lifetimes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Raw Pointer Problems
Definition

Memory leaks and dangling pointers

Manual allocation requires careful matching of every allocation and deallocation; exceptions and control flow make this error-prone.

Common mistake
Allocating with new and forgetting to delete, or deleting then continuing to use a pointer.
Why it matters
These bugs can crash programs or silently consume resources, degrading reliability and performance.
Key Takeaway

Avoid manual lifetime bookkeeping. Prefer patterns that guarantee cleanup even on early return or exceptions.

Illustration
// Minimal leak example
#include <iostream>

struct Box {
  Box() { std::cout << "Box created" << std::endl; }
  ~Box(){ std::cout << "Box destroyed" << std::endl; }
};

int main() {
  Box* p = new Box(); // allocated
  // ... early return or error happens before delete
  return 0; // destructor never called, memory leaked
}
Concrete example
If an exception is thrown after allocation but before delete, the destructor is never invoked and the memory is lost.
Check your understanding
Ask: where would you add a destructor or RAII wrapper to guarantee cleanup in this code?

screens.title: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII)
screens.narratorSegment: RAII is the idiom that turns resource management into deterministic object lifetime management. The claim is simple: acquire a resource in a constructor and release it in the destructor. That means when an object goes out of scope—either normally, by return, or because an exception escaped—its destructor runs and the resource is freed. This applies to memory, files, locks, sockets, and more. A standard library example is std::ofstream: open the file in the constructor, and when the stream object is destroyed it closes the file automatically. The practical advantage is that you no longer have to manually track every code path: RAII centralizes resource cleanup in object destructors. A common misconception is that RAII only helps with simple cases. In fact, RAII scales because you can compose RAII types. You can wrap C-style handles with unique_ptr and a custom deleter to get RAII semantics. In the assessment example, std::ofstream demonstrates RAII for file handles: if writing throws, the destructor still closes the file, preventing resource leaks. Think of RAII as moving cleanup from ad-hoc calls into language-guaranteed object lifetimes. Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) means tie acquisition to construction and release to destruction so cleanup happens automatically in all control flows, including exceptions.. In practical terms, a single pattern that guarantees cleanup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › RAII Explained
Definition

Resource Acquisition Is Initialization

RAII binds resource lifetime to object lifetime so objects clean up in their destructors automatically.

  • Constructor acquires the resource.
  • Destructor releases it no matter how scope ends.
  • Works for memory, files, locks, and other handles.
Key Takeaway

Prefer RAII wrappers for resources so cleanup does not depend on manual calls spread across code paths.

Practical example
#include <iostream>
#include <fstream>
#include <stdexcept>

void createAndProcessFile(const std::string& filename) {
  std::ofstream outFile(filename); // File opened in constructor (resource acquired)
  if (!outFile.is_open()) {
    throw std::runtime_error("Failed to open file");
  }
  outFile << "First line" << std::endl;
  // If an exception is thrown here, outFile's destructor still runs and closes the file.
}
Concrete scenario
A file write fails after allocation. RAII ensures the file handle is closed even when the write throws.
Misconception
RAII does not prevent logic bugs; it guarantees deterministic cleanup for resources it manages.

screens.title: std::unique_ptr — exclusive ownership
screens.narratorSegment: std::unique_ptr enforces exclusive ownership of a dynamically allocated object. The essential rules: it cannot be copied, only moved, and its destructor deletes the object it owns. That makes unique_ptr an ideal RAII wrapper when exactly one owner should control lifetime. The preferred creation method is std::make_unique because it provides exception safety and clearer syntax. In practice you create a unique_ptr with make_unique, and when you need to transfer ownership you use std::move. A common pattern is to pass unique_ptr by value into functions when you want the callee to take ownership; otherwise, pass by reference to avoid transfer. A misconception is that get() is safe to use for lifetime management; get() returns a raw pointer for observation only and does not change ownership — deleting that raw pointer will cause a double-free. Use unique_ptr::release only when you intentionally want to relinquish ownership and manage the resource manually, which is rare. The included code demonstrates creation, moving ownership, and what happens when the owner goes out of scope and the object is destroyed. Practice by observing constructor and destructor messages to confirm single ownership semantics.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › std::unique_ptr
Concept

Exclusive ownership

Only one unique_ptr owns an object at a time. The destructor deletes the object automatically.

  • Prefer std::make_unique to construct.
  • Use std::move to transfer ownership.
  • Avoid manual delete of raw pointers obtained from get().
Key Takeaway

unique_ptr makes ownership explicit and prevents accidental sharing and double deletion.

Code Walkthrough
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

class MyResource {
public:
  MyResource(const std::string& name) : name_(name) { std::cout << "MyResource " << name_ << " created." << std::endl; }
  ~MyResource(){ std::cout << "MyResource " << name_ << " destroyed." << std::endl; }
  void doSomething(){ std::cout << "MyResource " << name_ << " is doing something." << std::endl; }
private:
  std::string name_;
};

int main() {
  auto resource1 = std::make_unique<MyResource>("A");
  resource1->doSomething();

  auto resource2 = std::move(resource1); // transfer ownership
  if (!resource1) { std::cout << "resource1 is now null." << std::endl; }
  resource2->doSomething();

  // resource2 destroyed automatically when it goes out of scope
}
Concrete example
Moving resource1 into resource2 shows ownership transfer and that only one destructor runs.
Common mistake
Calling delete on a raw pointer returned by get() will cause double-free when the unique_ptr later deletes it.

screens.title: Passing unique_ptr to functions
screens.narratorSegment: How you pass unique_ptr to functions determines ownership semantics. If the callee must take ownership, pass the unique_ptr by value and use std::move at the call site. That transfers ownership and ensures the callee becomes responsible for the resource. If the callee only needs to observe or operate without taking ownership, pass a raw pointer or reference obtained via get() or pass a reference to the unique_ptr itself. But be careful: a raw pointer from get() is only for observation; it doesn't extend lifetime. Also consider passing a reference to the unique_ptr when you want the callee to possibly reset it. A common pattern is to write a function that accepts std::unique_ptr<T> by value and performs work, ensuring the resource is destroyed when the function ends. The process example from the chapter demonstrates transferring ownership into a function. The misconception to watch out for is expecting the source pointer to remain valid after a move. After std::move, the source becomes null and must not be dereferenced. Testing these flows with constructor/destructor messages clarifies when objects are destroyed. Passing unique_ptr to functions means pass unique_ptr by value to transfer ownership, or pass a pointer/reference to observe without transfer; moving nulls the source.. In practical terms, transfer ownership or observe safely without transfer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › unique_ptr Function Patterns
Pattern

Transfer vs Observe

Decide if the function should own the resource or just use it temporarily.

Transfer ownership
Accept std::unique_ptr by value and call with std::move to hand off ownership.
Observe only
Pass a raw pointer or a reference. Remember the caller still controls lifetime.
Common Mistake

After moving, do not use the original pointer. It no longer owns the resource and may be null.

Example
void processResource(std::unique_ptr<MyResource> res) {
  // res now owns the resource; it will be destroyed when res goes out of scope
  res->doSomething();
}

int main() {
  auto resource = std::make_unique<MyResource>("A");
  processResource(std::move(resource)); // ownership transferred
  // resource is now null
}
Concrete scenario
Pass ownership of a socket or file handle to a worker function that is responsible for closing it.
Pro tip
If you don't want transfer, prefer const reference or raw pointer for observation only.

screens.title: std::shared_ptr — shared ownership and reference counting
screens.narratorSegment: std::shared_ptr implements shared ownership through reference counting. Each shared_ptr shares a control block that contains a reference counter. When you copy a shared_ptr, the counter increments; when a shared_ptr is destroyed or reset, the counter decrements. The managed object is deleted when the counter reaches zero. This model is useful when multiple components need to keep an object alive independently. std::make_shared is the preferred creation pattern because it can allocate the control block and object together, improving performance and exception safety. An important diagnostic tool is the use_count method, which returns the current number of owners; tracking use_count while copying into containers or passing to functions helps you reason about lifetime. But remember that use_count is a snapshot and can change concurrently in multi-threaded contexts unless synchronized. Also be mindful of the overhead: shared_ptr incurs atomic reference updates and a control block, so use it where shared ownership is genuinely required. In the included example we construct shared pointers, copy them, push into a vector, and observe how the ref count changes at each step. Watch destructor messages to confirm when the object is finally destroyed.

keyIdea.text: Use shared_ptr when ownership must be shared; the object is freed only when the reference count drops to zero.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › std::shared_ptr
Definition

Reference-counted ownership

A shared_ptr increments a reference counter on copy; destruction decrements it and deletes the object when it hits zero.

  • Prefer std::make_shared for creation.
  • use_count shows current owner count (snapshot).
  • Be aware of overhead from reference counting.
Key Takeaway

shared_ptr keeps objects alive while any owner exists, but shared ownership should be used intentionally.

Code Example
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>
#include <string>

class MyOtherResource {
public:
  MyOtherResource(const std::string& name) : name_(name) { std::cout << "MyOtherResource " << name_ << " created." << std::endl; }
  ~MyOtherResource(){ std::cout << "MyOtherResource " << name_ << " destroyed." << std::endl; }
  void doSomething(){ std::cout << "MyOtherResource " << name_ << " is doing something." << std::endl; }
private:
  std::string name_;
};

int main() {
  auto sharedRes1 = std::make_shared<MyOtherResource>("B");
  std::cout << "sharedRes1 ref count: " << sharedRes1.use_count() << std::endl;

  auto sharedRes2 = sharedRes1; // copies increments ref count
  std::cout << "sharedRes1 ref count: " << sharedRes1.use_count() << std::endl;

  std::vector<std::shared_ptr<MyOtherResource>> resources;
  resources.push_back(sharedRes1); // ref count increments
  std::cout << "sharedRes1 ref count after vector push: " << sharedRes1.use_count() << std::endl;
}
Concrete example
Copies and container pushes increase use_count; object destruction is delayed until the count reaches zero.
Misconception
use_count is not a synchronization tool. In concurrent code the count may change between calls.

screens.title: When to use unique_ptr vs shared_ptr
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between unique_ptr and shared_ptr is ultimately a design decision about ownership intent. Use unique_ptr when a single component logically owns a resource and is responsible for its lifetime. This gives clear performance and safety benefits since there's no reference counting overhead, and ownership transfer is explicit through move. Choose shared_ptr when many different parts of the program need to keep an object alive independently, for example when multiple callbacks or data structures must co-own an object. Shared_ptr simplifies lifetime management but introduces reference counting and potential performance costs. A common misconception is to use shared_ptr everywhere to avoid thinking about ownership. That can hide design problems and add unnecessary overhead. Prefer unique_ptr by default and elevate to shared_ptr only when sharing is required. When sharing creates graph-like relationships, consider whether weak_ptr is necessary to avoid circular references. The comparison here shows the trade-offs and practical rules: default to unique_ptr, reach for shared_ptr when lifetime must outlive any single owner, and use weak_ptr to express observation without ownership. When to use unique_ptr vs shared_ptr means default to unique_ptr for single ownership; use shared_ptr only for true shared lifetime needs and weak_ptr to avoid cycles.. In practical terms, ownership intent shapes your pointer choice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Choosing between unique_ptr and shared_ptr is ultimately a design decision about ownership intent. Use unique_ptr when a single component logically owns a resource and is responsible for its lifetime. This gives clear performance and safety benefits since there's no reference counting overhead, and ownership transfer is explicit through move. Choose shared_ptr when many different parts of the program need to keep an object alive independently, for example when multiple callbacks or data structures must co-own an object. Shared_ptr simplifies lifetime management but introduces reference counting and potential performance costs. A common misconception is to use shared_ptr everywhere to avoid thinking about ownership. That can hide design problems and add unnecessary overhead. Prefer unique_ptr by default and elevate to shared_ptr only when sharing is required. When sharing creates graph-like relationships, consider whether weak_ptr is necessary to avoid circular references. The comparison here shows the trade-offs and practical rules: default to unique_ptr, reach for shared_ptr when lifetime must outlive any single owner, and use weak_ptr to express observation without ownership. When to use unique_ptr vs shared_ptr means default to unique_ptr for single ownership; use shared_ptr only for true shared lifetime needs and weak_ptr to avoid cycles.. In practical terms, ownership intent shapes your pointer choice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › unique_ptr vs shared_ptr
Quick comparison
unique_ptr
Exclusive ownership, move-only, no reference counting, prefer by default.
shared_ptr
Shared ownership with reference counting. Use when multiple independent owners exist.
Decision guide

Prefer unique_ptr for clear ownership; use shared_ptr when life must be extended by many owners; use weak_ptr to break cycles.

Concrete trade-offs
  • Performance: unique_ptr is lighter, shared_ptr uses a control block and atomic ops.
  • Safety: both provide RAII guarantees; shared_ptr delays destruction until all owners release.
  • Design: unique_ptr clarifies a single clear owner in APIs; shared_ptr hides ownership across multiple components.
Misconception
Using shared_ptr everywhere simplifies passing but can mask flawed ownership design and add runtime cost.

screens.title: Circular dependencies and the leak problem
screens.narratorSegment: A circular dependency occurs when two or more objects hold strong shared_ptr references to each other. Each object increments the other's reference count, so even when external owners release their shared_ptrs, the internal cycle keeps the counts above zero and prevents destruction. This is a classic memory leak with shared ownership. The example of a doubly linked structure with shared_ptr for both next and prev demonstrates the issue: node1 owns node2 and node2 owns node1, their ref counts never reach zero. Developers sometimes misunderstand that shared_ptr always frees memory: it does, but only when the reference count drops to zero. Breaking cycles requires making one side non-owning. That's where std::weak_ptr enters: it points without owning and does not increment the reference count. After an owning shared_ptr is reset, weak_ptr lets you detect expiration safely via lock(). The practical rule is to avoid mutual strong ownership; make back-references or caches weak. This prevents invisible leaks and lets destructors run as expected. Circular dependencies and the leak problem means mutual shared_ptr ownership creates a reference cycle that prevents destructors from running. use weak_ptr to break the cycle.. In practical terms, why two shared owners can prevent destruction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Circular Dependencies
Problem

Mutual strong ownership

If two objects hold shared_ptrs to each other, their ref counts never drop to zero and destructors are never called.

Example pitfall
Doubly linked nodes that hold shared_ptr for prev and next will leak if both ends keep strong references.
Warning

Shared ownership without breaking cycles is a subtle memory leak that standard tools may not catch easily.

Illustration (bad)
// Demonstration of problematic ownership
class BadNode {
public:
  std::shared_ptr<BadNode> next;
  std::shared_ptr<BadNode> prev; // strong back-reference creates cycle
};

int main() {
  auto a = std::make_shared<BadNode>();
  auto b = std::make_shared<BadNode>();
  a->next = b;
  b->prev = a; // cycle: a and b keep each other alive
}
Check your understanding
Ask: which pointer should be weak to safely allow destruction when external owners release the nodes?

screens.title: std::weak_ptr — non-owning references and lock()
screens.narratorSegment: std::weak_ptr provides a non-owning reference to an object managed by shared_ptr. Crucially, weak_ptr does not increment the shared object's reference count, so it does not prevent destruction. To access the underlying object, you call lock(), which returns a shared_ptr. If the object still exists, lock returns a non-empty shared_ptr and extends its lifetime for that scope; if the object has been destroyed, lock returns an empty shared_ptr. This pattern is essential for building graphs, caches, or back-references where you want to observe another object without owning it. The chapter's Node example shows a shared_ptr for next and a weak_ptr for prev. When the primary owner is reset, lock will safely indicate the previous node is gone. A common misconception is that weak_ptr automatically upgrades to shared ownership; it does not. You must call lock and check the result. Use weak_ptr intentionally for non-owning links to prevent reference cycles and allow deterministic cleanup. std::weak_ptr — non-owning references and lock() means weak_ptr observes without owning; use lock() to obtain a temporary shared_ptr and check for expiration safely.. In practical terms, break cycles with weak_ptr and safely obtain a shared_ptr with lock. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › std::weak_ptr
Concept

Non-owning reference

weak_ptr points to a shared_ptr-managed object but does not increase its use count, avoiding cycles.

  • Use lock() to attempt a temporary shared_ptr.
  • Check the returned shared_ptr before dereferencing.
  • Common for back-references or caches where ownership should not be transferred.
Key Takeaway

Use weak_ptr to express observation without ownership and call lock() to safely access the object if it still exists.

Code Example
class Node {
public:
  std::string name;
  std::shared_ptr<Node> next;
  std::weak_ptr<Node> prev; // weak to break circular ownership

  Node(const std::string& n) : name(n) { std::cout << "Node " << name << " created." << std::endl; }
  ~Node(){ std::cout << "Node " << name << " destroyed." << std::endl; }
};

int main() {
  auto a = std::make_shared<Node>("A");
  auto b = std::make_shared<Node>("B");
  a->next = b;
  b->prev = a; // weak_ptr doesn't increment ref count
  a.reset(); // A destroyed when its shared_ptr count drops to zero
}
Concrete scenario
Use weak_ptr for parent pointers or caches to avoid keeping objects alive unintentionally.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Graph Node Activity
Activity

Build nodes and connect neighbors

Define Node with name and vector<shared_ptr<Node>> neighbors. Use make_shared to create nodes and push neighbors into the vector.

Implementation checklist
Constructor/destructor logs, addNeighbor method, create three nodes in main, connect A->B, A->C, B->C, run and observe ref counts and destructions.
Extension
Add back-references as weak_ptr and watch how destruction proceeds when main resets owners.
Key Takeaway

This lab shows how shared ownership in containers affects lifetime and when weak_ptr is necessary to avoid leaks.

Starter code
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class Node {
public:
  std::string name;
  std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Node>> neighbors;
  Node(const std::string& n) : name(n) { std::cout << "Node '" << name << "' created." << std::endl; }
  ~Node(){ std::cout << "Node '" << name << "' destroyed." << std::endl; }
  void addNeighbor(std::shared_ptr<Node> neighbor) {
    neighbors.push_back(neighbor);
    std::cout << "  Node '" << name << "' added neighbor '" << neighbor->name << "'." << std::endl;
  }
};

int main() {
  auto nodeA = std::make_shared<Node>("A");
  auto nodeB = std::make_shared<Node>("B");
  auto nodeC = std::make_shared<Node>("C");

  nodeA->addNeighbor(nodeB);
  nodeA->addNeighbor(nodeC);
  nodeB->addNeighbor(nodeC);

  // Observe destructor calls when main exits
}

screens.title: Safety notes and custom deleters
screens.narratorSegment: Smart pointers reduce many classes of bugs, but they are not a silver bullet. One frequent mistake is mixing raw delete with smart pointers: never call delete on a pointer managed by a smart pointer. That will likely cause a double-free when the smart pointer later runs its destructor. Another safety note is about get() which provides a raw observing pointer; do not take ownership from it. Custom deleters are an advanced but important tool: all smart pointers accept a custom deleter so you can manage non-new resources safely, for example when a C A P I returns a FILE* that must be closed with fclose. You can wrap that handle in a unique_ptr with a deleter that calls fclose. This gives RAII semantics for resources not allocated with new. Finally, keep performance in mind: shared_ptr has atomic reference updates and a control block, so reserve shared_ptr for true shared lifetime needs. The practical rule remains: default to unique_ptr, use shared_ptr when needed, use weak_ptr to break cycles, and use custom deleters to adapt RAII to non-standard resources. Safety notes and custom deleters means don't delete smart-managed pointers manually, avoid taking ownership from get(), and use custom deleters for non-new resources.. In practical terms, avoid mixing raw and smart pointers and handle special resources correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Safety Notes & Custom Deleters
Common mistakes
Deleting a smart-managed pointer
Never call delete on a raw pointer obtained from a smart pointer; let the smart pointer own destruction.
Misusing get()
get() returns an observing pointer only. Do not use it to transfer ownership.
Pro tip

Wrap C handles with a smart pointer and a custom deleter to gain RAII behavior for non-new resources.

Custom deleter example
#include <memory>
#include <cstdio>

struct FileCloser { void operator()(std::FILE* f) const { if (f) std::fclose(f); } };

int main() {
  std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser> file(std::fopen("out.txt","w"));
  // file will be closed by FileCloser when the unique_ptr is destroyed
}
Concrete scenario
When interfacing C libraries that return opaque handles, use smart pointers with custom deleters to ensure RAII semantics.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate the main ideas you should carry forward. First, raw pointers require manual lifetime management and lead to memory leaks and dangling pointers when mishandled. Second, RAII ties resource acquisition to object construction and release to destruction, making cleanup automatic and exception-safe. Third, std::unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership, cannot be copied, and should be created with make_unique and transferred with move. Fourth, std::shared_ptr implements shared ownership with reference counting; use it when multiple owners must keep an object alive. Finally, std::weak_ptr is a non-owning observer used to break circular dependencies and safely test whether a shared object still exists by calling lock. Keep the rule of thumb: prefer unique_ptr by default, use shared_ptr only when needed, and use weak_ptr to avoid cycles. These patterns, combined with custom deleters for non-new resources, give you practical, testable ways to eliminate common lifetime bugs in C++.

Raw Pointer Problems

RAII
Acquire in constructor, release in destructor — guaranteed cleanup even on exceptions.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Practical Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Use this checklist when you edit or design interfaces. First, ask who should own the resource. If a single component owns it, prefer unique_ptr and make ownership transfer explicit with move. Second, when multiple independent owners must keep an object alive, use shared_ptr and track use_count during debugging to reason about lifetimes. Third, avoid mutual shared ownership—use weak_ptr for back-references, caches, or observers to prevent cycles. Fourth, prefer make_unique and make_shared to gain exception safety and potential allocation benefits. Fifth, wrap platform or C-style handles in smart pointers with custom deleters to get RAII for resources that are not allocated with new. Finally, never manually delete a pointer that a smart pointer manages. These simple checks will help you apply smart pointers correctly and prevent the most common lifetime mistakes in C++ code.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn why raw pointers create fragile programs and how smart pointers, using the RAII principle, make resource management automatic and reliable. You'll see the two main ownership models: exclusive ownership with unique pointers, and shared ownership with reference-counted shared pointers. We will also examine the subtle circular dependency problem that can occur with shared ownership and how weak pointers provide a carefully scoped, non-owning reference to solve it. Along the way we'll walk through real C++ examples that show construction, destruction, transfer of ownership, and reference counting in action. You will understand when to prefer make_unique or make_shared, how move semantics preserve exclusive ownership, and when to opt for weak_ptr to break cycles. By the end, you'll know practical rules of thumb for choosing the right smart pointer for file handles, graph nodes, containers, and APIs. This knowledge reduces memory leaks, eliminates dangling pointers, and makes your code safer under exceptions. Ready to see how RAII turns lifetime management from a manual chore into a design principle you can rely on? Let's explore the key topics and examples that will make this concrete.

These objectives guide our practice so you can measure real competency. First, you'll identify the common hazards of raw pointers: memory leaks when delete is forgotten, and dangling pointers when memory is accessed after deletion. Recognizing these bugs is the first step to avoiding them. Second, you'll explain the RAII principle: acquire a resource in a constructor and release it in the destructor. This single idea underpins reliable cleanup even when exceptions are thrown. Third, you'll implement and use std::unique_ptr for exclusive ownership: create objects with make_unique, move ownership, and avoid copies. That gives you a safe replacement for raw pointers when a single object owns a resource. Fourth, you'll implement and use std::shared_ptr and std::weak_ptr: observe how shared_ptr increments and decrements a reference counter, know when shared ownership is appropriate, and use weak_ptr to break circular references. Each skill is paired with code examples and a small mnemonic to help you choose the right pointer type in practical contexts. By training these four skills you reduce leaks and make C++ lifetimes explicit and maintainable.

In this continuation we'll focus on applying the objectives through code patterns and tests. You will practice creating nodes, transferring ownership, and observing destructor output to confirm correct lifetimes. For unique_ptr you'll build examples that use move semantics and check that the original pointer becomes null after transfer. For shared_ptr you'll track use_count as copies and container pushes change the reference counter. For weak_ptr you'll run a linked example where a back-reference is weak, then reset a shared owner and observe safe expiration. We'll also compare make_unique and make_shared: both are exception-safe, but make_shared can be more efficient because it allocates control block and object together. Finally, you'll learn common pitfalls: never delete a raw pointer managed by a smart pointer, and consider custom deleters when wrapping C handles. These practice goals map directly to the milestones from the previous screen, so you have clear, verifiable tasks to confirm competency.

Before we adopt smart pointers, we must understand what can go wrong with raw pointers. Raw pointers require manual calls to delete for every new. Forgetting a delete produces a memory leak: the program holds memory it no longer needs and never returns it to the system. Over time, leaks accumulate and can exhaust memory. Another hazard is dangling pointers: if memory is deleted but a pointer still refers to that address, dereferencing it causes undefined behavior and can crash the program. These bugs are often intermittent and hard to trace. A common debugging pattern is to add logging in constructors and destructors to observe when objects are freed, but prevention is better than diagnosis. Consider this minimal example that intentionally leaks memory. It allocates, but never releases the object. Run this small program in a controlled environment to watch how destructor messages never appear and how memory remains allocated. The key takeaway is that manual pairing of new and delete is error-prone, especially across exceptions, early returns, or complex control flow. That fragility is the reason RAII and smart pointers are such powerful patterns: they move cleanup out of your head and into object lifetimes.

RAII is the idiom that turns resource management into deterministic object lifetime management. The claim is simple: acquire a resource in a constructor and release it in the destructor. That means when an object goes out of scope—either normally, by return, or because an exception escaped—its destructor runs and the resource is freed. This applies to memory, files, locks, sockets, and more. A standard library example is std::ofstream: open the file in the constructor, and when the stream object is destroyed it closes the file automatically. The practical advantage is that you no longer have to manually track every code path: RAII centralizes resource cleanup in object destructors. A common misconception is that RAII only helps with simple cases. In fact, RAII scales because you can compose RAII types. You can wrap C-style handles with unique_ptr and a custom deleter to get RAII semantics. In the assessment example, std::ofstream demonstrates RAII for file handles: if writing throws, the destructor still closes the file, preventing resource leaks. Think of RAII as moving cleanup from ad-hoc calls into language-guaranteed object lifetimes. Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) means tie acquisition to construction and release to destruction so cleanup happens automatically in all control flows, including exceptions.. In practical terms, a single pattern that guarantees cleanup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

std::unique_ptr enforces exclusive ownership of a dynamically allocated object. The essential rules: it cannot be copied, only moved, and its destructor deletes the object it owns. That makes unique_ptr an ideal RAII wrapper when exactly one owner should control lifetime. The preferred creation method is std::make_unique because it provides exception safety and clearer syntax. In practice you create a unique_ptr with make_unique, and when you need to transfer ownership you use std::move. A common pattern is to pass unique_ptr by value into functions when you want the callee to take ownership; otherwise, pass by reference to avoid transfer. A misconception is that get() is safe to use for lifetime management; get() returns a raw pointer for observation only and does not change ownership — deleting that raw pointer will cause a double-free. Use unique_ptr::release only when you intentionally want to relinquish ownership and manage the resource manually, which is rare. The included code demonstrates creation, moving ownership, and what happens when the owner goes out of scope and the object is destroyed. Practice by observing constructor and destructor messages to confirm single ownership semantics.

How you pass unique_ptr to functions determines ownership semantics. If the callee must take ownership, pass the unique_ptr by value and use std::move at the call site. That transfers ownership and ensures the callee becomes responsible for the resource. If the callee only needs to observe or operate without taking ownership, pass a raw pointer or reference obtained via get() or pass a reference to the unique_ptr itself. But be careful: a raw pointer from get() is only for observation; it doesn't extend lifetime. Also consider passing a reference to the unique_ptr when you want the callee to possibly reset it. A common pattern is to write a function that accepts std::unique_ptr<T> by value and performs work, ensuring the resource is destroyed when the function ends. std::shared_ptr implements shared ownership through reference counting. Each shared_ptr shares a control block that contains a reference counter. When you copy a shared_ptr, the counter increments; when a shared_ptr is destroyed or reset, the counter decrements. The managed object is deleted when the counter reaches zero. This model is useful when multiple components need to keep an object alive independently. std::make_shared is the preferred creation pattern because it can allocate the control block and object together, improving performance and exception safety. An important diagnostic tool is the use_count method, which returns the current number of owners; tracking use_count while copying into containers or passing to functions helps you reason about lifetime. But remember that use_count is a snapshot and can change concurrently in multi-threaded contexts unless synchronized. Also be mindful of the overhead: shared_ptr incurs atomic reference updates and a control block, so use it where shared ownership is genuinely required. Choosing between unique_ptr and shared_ptr is ultimately a design decision about ownership intent. Use unique_ptr when a single component logically owns a resource and is responsible for its lifetime. This gives clear performance and safety benefits since there's no reference counting overhead, and ownership transfer is explicit through move. Choose shared_ptr when many different parts of the program need to keep an object alive independently, for example when multiple callbacks or data structures must co-own an object. Shared_ptr simplifies lifetime management but introduces reference counting and potential performance costs. A common misconception is to use shared_ptr everywhere to avoid thinking about ownership. That can hide design problems and add unnecessary overhead. Prefer unique_ptr by default and elevate to shared_ptr only when sharing is required. When sharing creates graph-like relationships, consider whether weak_ptr is necessary to avoid circular references. The comparison here shows the trade-offs and practical rules: default to unique_ptr, reach for shared_ptr when lifetime must outlive any single owner, and use weak_ptr to express observation without ownership. A circular dependency occurs when two or more objects hold strong shared_ptr references to each other. Each object increments the other's reference count, so even when external owners release their shared_ptrs, the internal cycle keeps the counts above zero and prevents destruction. This is a classic memory leak with shared ownership. The example of a doubly linked structure with shared_ptr for both next and prev demonstrates the issue: node1 owns node2 and node2 owns node1, their ref counts never reach zero. Developers sometimes misunderstand that shared_ptr always frees memory: it does, but only when the reference count drops to zero. Breaking cycles requires making one side non-owning. That's where std::weak_ptr enters: it points without owning and does not increment the reference count. After an owning shared_ptr is reset, weak_ptr lets you detect expiration safely via lock(). The practical rule is to avoid mutual strong ownership; make back-references or caches weak. This prevents invisible leaks and lets destructors run as expected. Circular dependencies and the leak problem means mutual shared_ptr ownership creates a reference cycle that prevents destructors from running. use weak_ptr to break the cycle.. std::weak_ptr provides a non-owning reference to an object managed by shared_ptr. Crucially, weak_ptr does not increment the shared object's reference count, so it does not prevent destruction. To access the underlying object, you call lock(), which returns a shared_ptr. If the object still exists, lock returns a non-empty shared_ptr and extends its lifetime for that scope; if the object has been destroyed, lock returns an empty shared_ptr. This pattern is essential for building graphs, caches, or back-references where you want to observe another object without owning it. The chapter's Node example shows a shared_ptr for next and a weak_ptr for prev. When the primary owner is reset, lock will safely indicate the previous node is gone. A common misconception is that weak_ptr automatically upgrades to shared ownership; it does not. You must call lock and check the result. Smart pointers reduce many classes of bugs, but they are not a silver bullet. One frequent mistake is mixing raw delete with smart pointers: never call delete on a pointer managed by a smart pointer. That will likely cause a double-free when the smart pointer later runs its destructor. Another safety note is about get() which provides a raw observing pointer; do not take ownership from it. Custom deleters are an advanced but important tool: all smart pointers accept a custom deleter so you can manage non-new resources safely, for example when a C A P I returns a FILE* that must be closed with fclose. You can wrap that handle in a unique_ptr with a deleter that calls fclose. This gives RAII semantics for resources not allocated with new. Finally, keep performance in mind: shared_ptr has atomic reference updates and a control block, so reserve shared_ptr for true shared lifetime needs. The practical rule remains: default to unique_ptr, use shared_ptr when needed, use weak_ptr to break cycles, and use custom deleters to adapt RAII to non-standard resources. Let's consolidate the main ideas you should carry forward. First, raw pointers require manual lifetime management and lead to memory leaks and dangling pointers when mishandled. Second, RAII ties resource acquisition to object construction and release to destruction, making cleanup automatic and exception-safe. Third, std::unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership, cannot be copied, and should be created with make_unique and transferred with move. Fourth, std::shared_ptr implements shared ownership with reference counting; use it when multiple owners must keep an object alive. Finally, std::weak_ptr is a non-owning observer used to break circular dependencies and safely test whether a shared object still exists by calling lock. Keep the rule of thumb: prefer unique_ptr by default, use shared_ptr only when needed, and use weak_ptr to avoid cycles. These patterns, combined with custom deleters for non-new resources, give you practical, testable ways to eliminate common lifetime bugs in C++.

Use this checklist when you edit or design interfaces. First, ask who should own the resource. If a single component owns it, prefer unique_ptr and make ownership transfer explicit with move. Second, when multiple independent owners must keep an object alive, use shared_ptr and track use_count during debugging to reason about lifetimes. Third, avoid mutual shared ownership—use weak_ptr for back-references, caches, or observers to prevent cycles. Fourth, prefer make_unique and make_shared to gain exception safety and potential allocation benefits. Fifth, wrap platform or C-style handles in smart pointers with custom deleters to get RAII for resources that are not allocated with new. Finally, never manually delete a pointer that a smart pointer manages. These simple checks will help you apply smart pointers correctly and prevent the most common lifetime mistakes in C++ code.
